title: Cement, steel and engineering
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The Cement, Ispat and Engineering & Metal federations.
body:
Heavy industry has its own BMS federations: the **Akhil Bharatiya Cement Mazdoor Mahasangh**, the **Akhil Bharatiya Ispat Mazdoor Mahasangh** (steel) and the **Bharatiya Engineering & Metal Mazdoor Mahasangh**. These are industries in which a single plant can employ thousands of people and sustain an entire township, and in which a change in technology or ownership can alter the lives of a whole region.

## Steel

Steel is the oldest and most visible of the three. The Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL), the largest government-owned steel producer, runs five integrated steel plants: **Rourkela**, which was the country's first public sector integrated plant, **Bhilai** in Chhattisgarh, **Durgapur** and **Burnpur (IISCO)** in West Bengal, and **Bokaro** in Jharkhand. It also runs special steel plants, namely the Alloy Steel Plant at Durgapur, the Salem Steel Plant in Tamil Nadu and Visvesvaraya Iron and Steel at **Bhadravati** in Karnataka. The Government of India owns about 65 per cent of SAIL's equity, and the company was given Maharatna status in 2010, which gives it wider operational and financial autonomy. IISCO at Burnpur was taken over as a subsidiary in 1978 and merged into SAIL in 2006.

For the workers, a steel plant is a very particular workplace. Heat, molten metal, heavy cranes, gases and moving machinery make safety an everyday concern. Alongside the permanent workforce there is a large body of contract workers who do maintenance, handling, loading and many other tasks. Unions in the sector therefore raise a set of recurring questions:

- **Wage settlements.** In public sector steel, wages for non-executive employees are settled periodically through a joint negotiating committee of management and unions. Delays in settlement and arrears are a frequent point of friction.
- **Regularisation of contract workers.** Unions ask that workers doing permanent, perennial work should be made regular, or at least be paid and covered equally.
- **Disinvestment.** Proposals to sell or reduce the Government's holding in steel units are watched closely, because ownership affects employment and the continuation of township facilities.
- **Safety.** Accidents in blast furnaces, coke ovens and rolling mills have made safety audits and staffing in hazardous areas a regular demand.

Steel is also a strategic material, used in railways, defence, construction and manufacturing, and BMS argues that public sector plants should be strengthened, with investment in modernisation and capacity, rather than weakened. The modernisation of IISCO Burnpur, which involved an investment of about Rs 16,000 crore, is an example of the kind of expansion that unions say should be matched by attention to the workers who run it.

## Cement

Cement is a capital-intensive industry in which a modern plant, with its kilns and automated systems, needs fewer people than a steel mill of comparable value, but it still has a large contract workforce in quarrying, packing, loading and transport. The concerns of workers include:

- **Bipartite wage agreements.** In the cement industry, wages of permanent workers are settled by agreement between the employers' association and the unions' federations. One recent agreement, signed by the Cement Manufacturers' Association and two federations of cement workers, provided a total increase of Rs 5,750, in two parts: Rs 3,450 with effect from 1 April 2022 and Rs 2,300 from 1 April 2024, with revision of allowances. It covered permanent workers of the member companies, but not contract workers, for whom the unions continued discussions through the Chief Labour Commissioner. This last detail shows the structural problem of the industry: permanent employees may get a negotiated increase, while the contract workers, who do much of the physically heavy work, depend on separate settlements.
- **Dust-related health problems.** Workers in quarries, crushers, kilns and packing sections are exposed to fine dust over long periods, which makes protective equipment, regular medical examination and dust control a standing demand.
- **The status of contract workers** in plants and mines. Disputes over contract workers' wages and regularisation in cement have gone on for years. A local agreement reached in 2018 at an ACC plant in Maharashtra, as reported by IndustriALL, gave over 1,000 contract workers a retrospective wage increase and a contractor contribution to social security premiums, and also provided that if the contractor changed, the new contractor would honour the terms. Agreements of this type protect workers against a contractor's change, which is a common way for contract workers to lose their gains.

## Engineering and metal

This federation covers a wide range of factories, from large public sector firms making machinery, vehicles and equipment, to small units in industrial clusters that supply parts, tools and castings. The difference between the two ends is huge. In a large unit, the worker may have a regular pay scale, provident fund and a recognised union. In a small cluster unit, the same kind of skilled work may be done by a worker with no appointment letter, a wage that depends on the owner's goodwill, and no social security. This is the reason why the Engineering & Metal federation concentrates on wage fixation, the regularisation of workers who have been temporary for years, and the extension of provident fund and ESI to the smaller establishments.

## What the new legal framework means for these industries

The Labour Codes, which came into force on 21 November 2025, apply across all three industries. For heavy industry, three features deserve attention. First, the Code on Wages provides for a minimum wage and timely payment, which matters most for contract workers whose pay is often delayed. Second, the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code governs safety, health and working conditions in factories, and workers in hazardous processes look to its rules for medical examination and safety standards. Third, the Code on Social Security covers provident fund, ESI, gratuity and related benefits, and the question for contract workers is whether a principal employer will actually ensure that the contractor pays them. The rules framed by the Centre and the States will decide how these provisions work on the shop floor.

## The industry's common challenge

Technology has reduced the number of workers per unit of output. A new rolling mill or kiln may produce far more with far fewer hands than its predecessor. BMS believes that skill development and re-skilling are the practical answer, not a policy of ignoring the workers who are displaced. In concrete terms this means advance notice to unions before technology is introduced, training programmes during working hours, redeployment within the establishment where possible, and fair terms where a post is abolished.

## What remains to be done

The unions in these sectors have a clear agenda: the timely settlement of wage agreements in steel and cement, the extension of the benefits of those agreements to contract workers, protection of workers' health in dusty and hot environments, a firm position on disinvestment that involves consultation, and support for the small engineering units that employ many workers but offer few protections. The federations will continue to raise these in the bipartite forums of each industry and with the Government.

The test of progress, as Thengadi Ji put it, is whether the worker shares in it.
